title: Is this a good time to rent?
gist: A FRED-built ratio of the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index to the BLS CPI for rent of primary residence (both rebased to 100 in January 2015, tracked from 1975Q1 to 2026Q1) sits near historical peaks, implying US homeownership is unusually expensive relative to renting. Citing Dallas Fed research, the post argues the normalization comes through inflation — rents track inflation while nominal house prices lag, so real house prices fall sharply while real rents barely move.

themes.theme: Own-vs-rent ratio at a historical extreme

insights.claim: The US ratio of house prices to rents remains near historical peaks as of first quarter 2026, making renting the relatively better financial choice for housing on a cost basis.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A Fed-published affordability read that favors renting supports sustained rental demand and caps the marginal owner-occupier bid — watch residential rental operators versus for-sale homebuilder volumes.
insights.quote: The most recent measure of the cost of owning a home (vs. renting a home) remains near historical peaks, suggesting renting today is a relatively better financial choice for housing.

insights.claim: Homeownership costs relative to rents rose rapidly in 2020 and have stayed at high values ever since, per Dallas Fed index work replicated in FRED.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The dislocation is a discrete 2020 regime break that has not mean-reverted in roughly six years — a stretched spring, not a slow drift, and therefore a mean-reversion setup with unclear timing.
insights.quote: the rapid rise of homeownership costs in 2020 and the high values since then
insights.locator: Researchers at the Dallas Fed used price index data

insights.claim: The cost of owning a home and the cost of renting a home historically tend to move together, which makes the current wide gap the anomaly rather than a new baseline.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: If the two series are cointegrated over history, the current spread is a tradable convergence thesis rather than a permanent structural shift in housing.
insights.locator: Which is the better financial choice—owning or renting

themes.theme: The price-to-rent ratio as a decision rule

insights.claim: An indexed ratio of house prices to rents is a reusable rule for the buy-versus-rent decision: a high ratio means house prices are outgrowing rents and ownership is relatively expensive, while a low ratio means buying is comparatively the better deal.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A single public, free, quarterly-updating series can be used as a housing valuation gauge — treat extremes in it the way you would treat extremes in an equity earnings yield.
insights.quote: A high ratio means house prices are growing faster than rents, making homeownership a relatively more expensive proposition. A lower ratio means buying a home is a comparatively better deal.
insights.locator: A high ratio means house prices are growing

insights.claim: The ratio has exactly two paths back toward its historical average — the numerator (house prices) falls or the denominator (rent prices) rises — so a high reading does not by itself forecast a nominal house price crash.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Bears calling for a nominal housing collapse from this ratio are ignoring the rent-side adjustment channel; position for a grind, not a bust.
insights.quote: The ratio will become smaller if the numerator falls or the denominator rises.

insights.so_what: No vendor data required — this is a zero-cost, auditable housing valuation indicator any allocator can refresh and backtest in-house.

insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Robustness across two independent index constructions raises confidence enough to size a position on the housing valuation view.

insights.claim: Higher inflation mechanically pushes the house-price-to-rent ratio down toward its historical average because inflation raises rent prices relatively more than it raises house prices.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Inflation is bullish for rental cash flows and bearish for real home equity — a reason to prefer rent-collecting assets over owner-occupied housing exposure in a sticky-inflation regime.
insights.quote: Because inflation increases rent prices relatively more than house prices, higher inflation would drive the ratio down, closer to its historical average.

insights.claim: Dallas Fed research concludes that nominal house-price growth trails inflation while rents keep pace, so in real terms rents change very little but house prices fall sharply.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The expected correction is a real-terms erosion of home values, invisible in nominal price headlines — hedge housing exposure on a real, not nominal, basis.
insights.quote: Rents rise along with inflation, while nominal house-price growth trails inflation. On an inflation-adjusted basis, rents change very little, but house prices fall sharply.

insights.claim: The Dallas Fed report draws on both US and international data to identify the pattern and likely future evolution of an elevated house price-to-rent ratio, implying the dynamic is not US-specific.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: If the mean-reversion pattern is cross-country, the same rent-vs-own valuation screen can be applied to other developed housing markets and their listed landlords.

insights.claim: A Federal Reserve regional bank publication is willing to state that renting is currently the relatively better financial choice, an implicit challenge to the default assumption that buying a home is always the superior long-run financial decision.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Official-sector framing that normalizes renting can shift household tenure preference at the margin, a slow tailwind for rental housing demand and a headwind for first-time buyer formation.
